en: The Fifty Jātaka Stories,
Chapter on Niḷinikā.
2. The Ummādantī Jātaka “Whose residence is this, Sunanda, protected by a yellow brick wall? ...
[The rest of the verse follows] ...”
Who is this that is seen from afar like a crest of flame,
like a blaze upon the peak of a mountain in the sky?
Whose daughter is she, O Sunanda?
"Whose daughter-in-law is she, or perhaps whose wife?
Answer me quickly when asked:
is her husband still living, or is he no longer present?"
“I indeed know this, O lord of men:
whether by means of thought, or by death, or even by life—
O protector of the earth, that man belongs to you alone.”
Day and night, being diligent for that purpose,
he has become prosperous, flourishing, and well-grown;
O Lord of Men, he is one of your ministers.
“This is the wife of Abhipāraka, O King, whose name is Ummadantī. “O, o!
This is her name! he exclaimed.
What was done by me both with wisdom and with devotion was very well performed;
for at that time, while looking upon me,
she drove me mad and made me frantic.
She who on the full-moon day entered [the hut],
with eyes like those of a deer and limbs as beautiful as a white lotus—
on that day, I thought there were two full-moons.
Having seen her, dressed in garments of yellowish-white,
when she gazes at me, enticing me with her beautiful, lovely,
and charming brows and long eyelashes;
Stretching her limbs, she seems to steal my mind,
like a Kimpurisa woman born in the forest on the mountain;
for then she was large and dark-complexioned.
With her jeweled earrings displaced and wearing but a single garment,
the woman gazes about like a startled doe.
When indeed will those with copper-colored nails and fine hair,
with soft arms anointed with the essence of sandalwood, with rounded fingers and delicate, firm, tapering wrists, [embrace me]?
A beautiful woman shall appear from my head.
When indeed will the daughter of Tirīṭi— her waist slender, covered by a golden net— climb upon me?
She will embrace me with her tender arms,
like a māluvā creeper climbing a tree born in the Brahma-forest.
When indeed shall she, with her beautiful complexion reddened by lac-dye, [embrace me]?
Bindutthani, with skin like a white lotus,
will bring her face close to my face,
as a drunkard brings his bowl of liquor to the mouth of another drunkard.
When he saw him standing there,
all-auspicious and enchanting,
then, regarding his own mind—
I do not recognize anyone at all.
Having seen Umādaṇḍī, who was adorned with loosened jewel-earrings, I have lost my senses.
I do not sleep by day or night,
like one who has lost a thousand-fold fortune.
If Sakka were to grant me a boon, [I would choose this].
And may this boon be granted to me:
for one night or two nights,
may I be a ferryman.
“Having sported with Ummādantī,
I would then become King Sivi. “While I was paying homage to the beings, O Lord of Beings, they said:”
Having approached, the yakkha spoke these words:
"The king's mind is fixed on you, who drive him mad;
I give you to him—enjoy his company."
“My merit is destroyed and I am not immortal;
people would know this evil of mine,
and there would be great distress for my mind.”
"Even after giving away her beloved Ummadantī,
you did not bite her. "O Lord of Men,
there is no one other than you or me who can know all that has been done by karma."
“Eat the forest with its thickets that I have given to you,
Ummandatī, as your food, O King!
“The man who commits an evil deed...”
Thus he conceives, thinking "I am," while others likewise conceive;
beings see him performing this,
as do those men on earth who are disciplined.
Is there perhaps some other man on earth who could believe in this world, "I have no one dear to me"?
And for him, there would be intense distress of mind.
“Having given her away, you have now seized my beloved Ummadantī.
“Surely she is dear to me, O Lord of Men;
she is not unloved by me, O Protector of the Earth.”
“Go, venerable sir, toward Ummadantī;
like a lion, you shall enter the cave of the rock.
“The wise, though oppressed by their own suffering, do not [despair].”
They relinquish even actions that yield pleasant results;
though deluded or intoxicated by pleasure,
they do not engage in evil deeds.
“You indeed are both my mother and my father,
my husband, my lord, my sustainer, and my deity; I,
along with my children and wife, am your slave.”
"Do as you please, my lord, according to your desire.
"He who, thinking 'I am the master,' commits evil, and having done so, treats others with contempt;..."
By that he does not live a long life;
even the gods look upon him with suspicion because of his evil deed.
That which was given by owners to one who is a stranger—
Those who, established in the Dhamma, accept a gift—
both the recipients and the givers therein perform an action that has happiness as its fruit.
Is there perhaps some other man on earth who could believe in this world,
"I have no one dear to me," and yet suffer such intense distress of mind?
“Even after giving her away, she is still dear to me.
“She is surely dear to me, O Lord of Men;
she is not unloved by me, O Protector of the Earth.”
“Eat, O King, this Ummadantī whom I have given to you,
together with the forest thickets. “He who,
through his own suffering, [sees] the suffering of another...”
Or one bestows one’s own happiness through happiness; "As it is for me, so it is for others"—
he who knows thus understands the Dhamma.
Is there indeed any other man on earth who could believe in this world that "I do not love him"? And for him,
there would be intense distress of mind.
“Even after giving me my beloved Ummadantī, you did not bite her.
“O Lord of Men, you know that she is dear to me;
she is not unloved by me, O Protector of the Earth.”
“O Lord of Men, I give you what is dear;
O King, those who give what is dear obtain what is dear.
“Then indeed, I shall kill him!”
I have made myself the cause of my own desire;
for I cannot bring myself to slay the Dhamma with what is not-Dhamma.
“If you do not desire my mindfulness, O Lord of Men,
best of heroes among men;
I relinquish it for the sake of all people.”
“‘Since you have released him from me, you have called him back to me. ‘If you, O Katta, abandon one who is innocent and a protector,
it will lead to his own harm.’”
"Great indeed would be your reproach,
and you would have no faction within that city.
"I shall endure this reproach," [he replied].
“O protector of the earth, let all this— blame, praise, and censure— come to me. O Śibi,
do as you wish, according to your pleasure.”
“He who takes neither blame nor praise,
who accepts neither censure nor honor—
from him both glory and fortune depart.”
"Just as water flows from dry land,
so too whatever suffering and pleasure there is,
as well as the essence of the Dhamma and mental distress— from this [it all arises]."
“I shall answer all [questions] with my breast,
as the earth is for all things that are stationary and those that move.
“Excessive attachment to the Dhamma and mental distress...”
I desire the suffering of others to cease;
alone I shall bear this burden,
established in the Dhamma, without depriving anyone of anything.
“O Lord of Men, do not create an obstacle for me regarding this meritorious deed that leads to heaven;
with a mind full of faith, I give Ummadantī to you.”
“The king has given wealth to the brahmins at the sacrifice.
“Surely you are well-disposed toward me, Khatte;
both Ummadantī and you are my friends.”
“Both the gods and all the ancestors would reproach him who,
seeing evil, [still acts] for the sake of the future life.
“O King of the Śivis, they would not speak thus according to the Dhamma;”
“O people of the countryside, all of you together with the inhabitants of Sānegama:
eat this Ummadantī that I have given you;
let the king enjoy the forest along with its trees.”
“Truly, Kaccāna, you are well-disposed toward me;
you and I are friends who have been driven mad together.
And the Dhammas of the virtuous have been well-proclaimed.”
“The ocean’s tide is difficult to overstep.
“You are worthy of offerings, compassionate for our welfare;
you are the sustainer, the provider, and the protector of desires.”
“O King, she has been offered; indeed, she brings great fruit.
Accept her, who is maddened with desire for me.
“Truly, you are capable of accomplishing everything;”
My son Kattū practiced the Dhamma;
for who else here in this world of living beings,
a two-footed man at dawn, could be so skilled at securing your safety?
“You indeed are the best, you are unsurpassed;
you are the guardian of Dhamma, the knower of Dhamma, the wise one.
As a guardian of Dhamma, may you live for a long time!
"Teach me the Dhamma, O Protector of the Dhamma!
Therefore, O one who carries one across,
listen now to my words."
I shall teach you the Dhamma,
which has been practiced by the virtuous.
Excellent, O King who delights in the Dhamma!
Excellent is the person possessed of wisdom;
excellent is one who does not deceive friends;
the non-doing of evil is happiness.
In the realm of a king who is free from anger and established in the Dhamma,
people dwell in happiness.
In the gathering of cool shade,
I do not approve of this: action performed without due reflection is not good.
Or those who, having understood for themselves, act accordingly—
listen now to these similes of mine.
It is like cattle rushing forward...
When the leader goes crookedly,
they all go crookedly,
since the guide has gone crookedly.
In the same way, among human beings,
whoever is regarded as the best—
if that person practices unrighteousness—
How much more so the rest of the people;
the entire kingdom lies in suffering if the king is unrighteous.
If, among cattle crossing over,
the leader goes straight,
all the cows go straight.
When one has gone straight and upright—
just so it is with those among humans who are considered the best.
Thus, if the king practices the Dharma,
how much more so the rest of his people;
the entire kingdom dwells in happiness.
Even if one were a righteous king,
I would not seek immortality through unrighteousness.
Or even to conquer this entire earth,
whatever there may be among human beings— this is what one must strive for.
These treasures are found here:
cattle, slaves, gold,
clothing, and yellow sandalwood.
For the sake of female slaves, jewels, and gems,
or even for those things that the moon and sun protect for me,
I would not walk in unrighteousness.
I was born as a bull among the Sivi people.
Raṭṭhapāla has arisen as a leader for their welfare,
honoring the Dhamma of the Sivis.
Thus, reflecting only upon the Dhamma,
he does not fall under the power of his own mind.
"Truly, O Great King, you..."
Constant, free from calamity, and auspicious;
you shall rule for a long time,
for such is your wisdom.
We rejoice in this,
that you do not neglect the Dhamma;
for a kshatriya who neglects the Dhamma—
The lord falls from his kingdom.
Practice the Dharma, O Great King,
toward your mother and father, O Kshatriya.
Having practiced the Dhamma here,
O King, you will go to heaven.
Practice the Dhamma, Great King.
Toward sons and wives, O Kshatriya;
... [and so on] ... Practice the Dhamma, O Great King.
O Kṣatriya, among friends and relatives...
[and so forth] ... Practice the Dharma, O Great King.
In vehicles and in armies;
…pe… Practice the Dhamma, O Great King.
In villages and in market towns;
…pe… Practice the Dhamma, O Great King.
In kingdoms and in provinces...
Practice the Dhamma, O Great King.
And among recluses and brahmins;
…pe… Practice the Dhamma, O Great King.
O Kshatriya among birds and beasts...
Practice the Dharma, O Great King.
The Dhamma practiced brings happiness;
having practiced the Dhamma here,
O King, you will go to heaven.
Practice the Dhamma, O Great King;
together with Indra, the gods, and Brahmā,
they have reached heaven by means of well-practiced conduct.
“O King, do not be negligent regarding the Dhamma.
Thus ends the second Jātaka, the Ummādantī Jātaka.
